pos: v.t. (to devise, contrive, or produce something new, especially for the first time)
etymology: Latin invenire, to come upon, to find, from in-, upon, and venire, to come. To invent is, at root, to come upon something not previously found — a discovery that becomes, in later use, a deliberate act of devising.
biblical_def:
Amos's indictment of the complacent rich of Israel and Zion reaches its climax with a comparison that has embarrassed commentators for its sheer specificity: they chant to the sound of the viol, and invent to themselves instruments of musick, like David. The comparison to David is not incidental praise; it is the sharpest possible edge of the rebuke. David's own musical invention served the worship of the LORD, instruments devised for the tabernacle and later the temple, entire courses of Levites organized around his compositions. The men Amos condemns invent instruments for exactly the opposite use, entertainment at a banquet table while they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph, the northern kingdom's own approaching ruin.

What makes the passage bite is how ordinary and even impressive the invention itself is. Amos does not condemn musical creativity as such, nor does he compare these men to some obviously wicked model; he names David, the very man whose musical inventions Scripture elsewhere records with approval, and shows the identical creative gift, put to identical technical use, utterly damned by the moral vacancy surrounding it. An invention is judged, in this text, not by its ingenuity or its resemblance to a godly precedent, but by whether it accompanies grief for real affliction or merely provides better music to ignore it by.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to devise; to contrive; to produce something new, by the exercise of ingenuity or imagination.
webster_full: INVENT, v.t. To devise or contrive by original thought; to produce something new, not before known or existing.
CHANT, v.i. To sing, especially in a monotonous or melodious manner; to sing psalms or sacred music.
AFFLICTION, n. Distress; suffering; a state of pain, misfortune, or grief.
GRIEVE, v.i. To feel sorrow or grief; to mourn; to be distressed at some evil.
WOE, n. Grievous distress or calamity; an exclamation of denunciation or threatened judgment.
scriptures: Amo 6:4
That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall;
Amo 6:5
That chant to the sound of the viol, and invent to themselves instruments of musick, like David;
Amo 6:6
That drink wine in bowls, and anoint themselves with the chief ointments: but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph.
Moreover four thousand were porters; and four thousand praised the LORD with the instruments which I made, said David, to praise therewith.
corruption_summary: Creative invention is treated as morally neutral in itself, valued purely for skill or novelty, when Amos condemns an invention structurally identical to David's own for the single reason that it accompanies indifference to real affliction rather than worship or grief.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; to invent still means to devise something new. The principle worth recovering is exactly why Amos reaches for David as his comparison rather than some more obviously decadent figure. The technical act of inventing an instrument is presented as identical in both cases; what differs entirely is the moral context surrounding the invention.

David's own testimony in Chronicles shows instruments he made used specifically to praise the LORD, in the middle of an ordered, worshipful national life. Amos's condemned men invent with the same evident skill and creativity, in a banquet hall stocked with ivory beds and choice ointments, while a national catastrophe presses close and produces in them no grief at all. The lesson Amos presses is not against musical invention but against invention detached from moral attention — skill spent perfecting the soundtrack of indifference.
roots_summary: Hebrew chashab (H2803), to think, plan, devise; the verb behind “invent” in Amos 6:5, elsewhere used of both righteous and wicked scheming.
roots_lines: Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to think, plan, devise, invent; the verb rendered “invent” in Amos 6:5, morally neutral in itself and used of both good and evil planning elsewhere.
Hebrew nebel (H5035) — a viol, a stringed instrument, a skin-bottle; one of the instruments named in Amos's indictment.
Hebrew shever (H7667) — a breaking, a fracture, ruin; the underlying idea behind “affliction of Joseph,” the coming national breach.
Hebrew chalah (H2470, in the sense of being grieved or sick) — to be weak, sick, grieved; negated of these men, they are not grieved.
Hebrew shir (H7891/H7892) — to sing, a song; the standing verb and noun for the worship-music David's own instruments were made to accompany.
usage: “invent to themselves instruments of musick, like David” — Amos's sharpest comparison.
“they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph” — the moral vacancy the invention accompanied.
“four thousand praised the LORD with the instruments which I made, said David” — the same creative gift rightly used.

pos: a. (not restrained or governed by law; contrary to law; unprincipled)
etymology: Saxon lagu, law, with the privative suffix -less. A lawless man is, at root, one who lives as though no law applied to him at all, whether or not a law in fact exists.
biblical_def:
Paul's defense of the law's proper use, in his first letter to Timothy, produces a catalogue of the people the law is actually aimed at, opening with this word: the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners. The statement is a careful piece of theology, not a dismissal of the law. Paul has just affirmed, one verse earlier, that the law is good, if a man use it lawfully; his point is not that law is unnecessary but that its proper target is precisely the lawless man, the one living as though no restraint bound him.

The list that follows names lawlessness in its concrete, ugly particulars — murderers of fathers and mothers, manslayers, whoremongers, menstealers, liars, perjured persons — and closes with a phrase that refuses to let the list feel exhaustive: if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine. A righteous man, united to Christ by faith, is not under the law in the sense of standing condemned by it, since its accusing function finds nothing left in him to accuse once he is justified; the lawless man is exactly the one for whom the law's restraining and condemning function remains in full, undiminished force, precisely because nothing in him yet restrains himself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): not subject to law; unrestrained by law; contrary to law; disobedient to lawful authority.
webster_full: LAWLESS, a. Not subject to or restrained by law; contrary to law; unprincipled; ungoverned.
RIGHTEOUS, a. Just; upright; conforming to the divine law; free from guilt or sin.
DISOBEDIENT, a. Neglecting or refusing to obey; not submissive to authority or command.
SOUND, a. Free from error, defect, or corruption; here, of doctrine, wholesome and true.
GODLY, a. Pious; reverencing God and his laws; living in obedience to God's commands.
scriptures: But we know that the law is good, if a man use it lawfully;

Knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners, for unholy and profane, for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, for manslayers,
For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine;
Gal 3:24
Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith.
corruption_summary: The law is treated either as irrelevant to a believer or as the whole substance of righteousness, when Paul specifically locates its condemning force against the lawless man while pointing the righteous man toward the faith the law itself was meant to prepare him for.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; lawless still names one unrestrained by law. The principle worth recovering is the precision of Paul's own argument, easy to flatten in either of two directions. One error dismisses the law as having nothing to say to a Christian at all; the other treats law-keeping itself as the ground of righteousness the law was never meant to supply.

Paul's own resolution runs through Galatians as much as through this letter to Timothy: the law was a schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith, not the source of that justification itself. Its proper business remains restraining and exposing the lawless, disobedient, and ungodly exactly as 1 Timothy one describes; a righteous man is not thereby exempted from all moral obligation, but freed from the law's condemning terror precisely because Christ has already met its full demand in his place.
roots_summary: Greek anomos (G459), without law, lawless; the adjective behind “lawless” in 1 Timothy 1:9, from a-, without, and nomos, law.
roots_lines: Greek anomos (G459) — without law, lawless, unprincipled; the adjective rendered “lawless” in 1 Timothy 1:9.
Greek anupotaktos (G506) — unruly, not subject to authority; the word rendered “disobedient” in the same verse.
Greek asebes (G765) — ungodly, impious; naming the second category the law is aimed at.
Greek hugiainousa didaskalia (G5198/G1319) — sound doctrine, healthy teaching; the standard against which the whole catalogue is measured in verse 10.
Greek paidagogos (G3807) — a schoolmaster, a child-attendant; the figure Galatians 3:24 uses of the law's true, preparatory office.
usage: “the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient” — Paul's precise statement of the law's target.
“if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine” — the catalogue's deliberately open-ended close.
“the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ” — the law's true purpose, distinct from its restraint of the lawless.

pos: a. (pertaining to or given to idolatry; worshipping idols or false gods)
etymology: Greek eidololatres, from eidolon, an image or idol, and latreia, service or worship. An idolatrous man is, at root, one who has given the service owed to God alone to a mere image instead.
biblical_def:
Josiah's great reformation, recorded in the twenty-third chapter of Second Kings, names one particular class of officeholder among the many objects of the young king's purge: he put down the idolatrous priests, whom the kings of Judah had ordained to burn incense in the high places in the cities of Judah, and in the places round about Jerusalem. These were not foreign infiltrators but Judah's own appointed clergy, installed by previous kings of David's own line, whose entire office existed to serve idols under royal sanction — an institutionalized, generations-deep idolatry with its own ordained priesthood, its own budget, and its own standing in the cities of the covenant people.

Josiah's reform did not merely rebuke private idol-worship among the people; it dismantled an entire ordained apparatus, put down by his own royal authority precisely because it had been set up by royal authority in the first place. Hosea's earlier indictment, like people, like priest, supplies the theology behind the scale of the corruption Josiah found: a corrupted priesthood does not merely tolerate a corrupted people but actively forms and legitimizes it, generation after generation, until an idolatrous office looks, to those born under it, like ordinary and unremarkable religious life. Removing it required not persuasion but the plain exercise of covenant authority, putting down what covenant authority itself had wrongly put up.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): pertaining to idolatry; consisting in the worship of idols; addicted to the worship of false gods.
webster_full: IDOLATROUS, a. Consisting in idolatry; devoted to or practicing the worship of idols or images.
IDOLATRY, n. The worship of idols, images, or false gods; excessive attachment to any object in place of God.
REFORMATION, n. A change from worse to better; correction of error, abuse, or corruption, especially in religion.
ORDAIN, v.t. To appoint, establish, or set apart, especially to a religious office, by formal ceremony.
HIGH PLACE, n. An elevated site used for pagan worship or unauthorized sacrifice, condemned throughout the Old Testament.
scriptures: And the king commanded Hilkiah the high priest, and the priests of the second order, and the keepers of the door, to bring forth out of the temple of the LORD all the vessels that were made for Baal, and for the grove, and for all the host of heaven: and he burned them without Jerusalem in the fields of Kidron, and carried the ashes of them unto Bethel.

And he put down the idolatrous priests, whom the kings of Judah had ordained to burn incense in the high places in the cities of Judah, and in the places round about Jerusalem; them also that burned incense unto Baal, to the sun, and to the moon, and to the planets, and to all the host of heaven.
Hos 4:9
And there shall be, like people, like priest: and I will punish them for their ways, and reward them their doings.
And Hilkiah the high priest said unto Shaphan the scribe, I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD. And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it.
corruption_summary: Idolatry is imagined as an obviously foreign or crude error, easily recognized and avoided, when Josiah's reform confronts an idolatrous priesthood fully ordained, funded, and normalized within Judah's own royal and religious establishment for generations.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; idolatrous still names devotion to a false god. The principle worth recovering is how thoroughly institutionalized the idolatry Josiah confronted had become. These were not outsiders sneaking incense onto a hillside; they were ordained officeholders, appointed by the kings of Judah themselves, serving in the cities of the covenant people with the full apparatus of legitimate religious office.

Hosea's diagnosis, like people, like priest, names the mechanism by which such corruption becomes self-perpetuating: a priesthood that has normalized idolatry does not merely fail to correct the people, it actively forms them into its own image. Josiah's reform required the discovery of the actual book of the law, long lost in the temple itself, before the scale of the departure could even be recognized; the idolatrous priesthood had been standing so long and so respectably that recovering the standard by which to judge it was itself the first, necessary act of reform.
roots_summary: Hebrew kemarim (H3649), a rare and specific term for idolatrous priests; the word behind “idolatrous” in 2 Kings 23:5, distinct from the ordinary word for priest.
roots_lines: Hebrew kemarim (H3649) — idolatrous priests, a rare and pejorative term distinct from kohen, the ordinary word for priest; used only three times in the Old Testament.
Hebrew bamah (H1116) — a high place; the standing site of unauthorized worship these priests served at.
Hebrew qatar (H6999) — to burn incense, to make a sacrifice smoke; the specific priestly act these idolatrous officeholders performed.
Hebrew tsava' hashamayim — the host of heaven; the astral bodies worshipped alongside Baal in this same reform.
Hebrew sepher hattorah — the book of the law; its rediscovery in 2 Kings 22:8 is what precipitated Josiah's entire reform.
usage: “he put down the idolatrous priests, whom the kings of Judah had ordained” — Josiah's reform of institutionalized idolatry.
“like people, like priest” — Hosea's diagnosis of how such corruption perpetuates itself.
“I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD” — the rediscovery that made the reform possible.

pos: v.t. (to shut out; to hinder from participation, entrance, or inclusion)
etymology: Latin excludere, from ex-, out, and claudere, to shut. To exclude is, at root, to shut a door against someone from the outside, whether from a place, a group, or a relationship.
biblical_def:
Paul's letter to the Galatians names a specific and calculated purpose behind the false teachers troubling that church, using this word to expose it: They zealously affect you, but not well; yea, they would exclude you, that ye might affect them. The zeal these teachers show toward the Galatians is real, Paul concedes, but its aim is not the Galatians' good; it is to exclude them, cutting them off from Paul's own apostolic teaching and from the freedom of the gospel he had preached, precisely so that the Galatians would then be dependent on these new teachers alone, courting their favor instead.

The exclusion in view is relational and doctrinal rather than merely social — a deliberate severing of the Galatians from the source that had first brought them the true gospel, so that a false teacher could occupy the vacated position of authority. Paul's earlier question in the same passage, Am I therefore become your enemy, because I tell you the truth?, shows the exclusion working exactly as intended, turning a faithful apostle into a suspected outsider while the actual outsiders present themselves as the Galatians' truest friends. Scripture's warning here is precise: a zeal that works to exclude a believer from proven, faithful teaching, however warmly it courts that believer's own affection in return, is not zeal for the believer's good at all.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to shut out; to hinder from entering or participating; to debar or prevent from admission.
webster_full: EXCLUDE, v.t. To shut out; to prevent from entering, sharing, or participating; to debar.
ZEALOUS, a. Ardently devoted; filled with zeal, whether for a good or a bad end.
AFFECT, v.t. To have a strong liking or fondness for; also, to aim at, aspire to, or court favor with.
GOSPEL, n. The good news of salvation through Christ; the doctrine of grace preached by the apostles.
APOSTLE, n. One sent with a message or commission; specifically, one of Christ's chosen messengers of the gospel.
scriptures: Gal 4:16
Am I therefore become your enemy, because I tell you the truth?
Gal 4:17
They zealously affect you, but not well; yea, they would exclude you, that ye might affect them.
Gal 4:18
But it is good to be zealously affected always in a good thing, and not only when I am present with you.
Gal 1:6
I marvel that ye are so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ unto another gospel:
corruption_summary: Zealous, flattering attention is treated as proof of genuine care, when Paul exposes precisely this kind of zeal as a deliberate tactic to exclude believers from faithful teaching so a false teacher can claim their affection instead.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; to exclude still means to shut out. The principle worth recovering is Paul's careful separation of zeal from goodness — they zealously affect you, but not well. Real ardor, real attention, real apparent care can all be present in a relationship whose actual purpose is to cut a believer off from the truth rather than to build them up in it.

The tactic's success is visible in the very question Paul has to ask, am I therefore become your enemy, because I tell you the truth? An exclusion that works turns the faithful teacher into the suspect and the excluding teacher into the trusted friend. Paul's own remedy is not to condemn zeal as such, since he affirms in the next verse that it is good to be zealously affected always in a good thing, but to insist that the test of any zeal directed at a believer is not its warmth but whether it draws them toward the true gospel or excludes them from it.
roots_summary: Greek ekkleio (G1576), to shut out, to exclude; the verb of Galatians 4:17, from ek-, out, and kleio, to shut.
roots_lines: Greek ekkleio (G1576) — to shut out, exclude; used only at Galatians 4:17 and Romans 3:27 in the New Testament.
Greek zeloo (G2206) — to be zealous, to court earnestly, sometimes with a negative sense of jealous courting; the verb behind “zealously affect.”
Greek kalos (G2573, negated) — good, well, rightly; explicitly denied of the false teachers' zeal, not well.
Greek metatithemi (G3346) — to transfer, remove, change allegiance; the verb behind “so soon removed” in Galatians 1:6.
Greek euangelion (G2098) — good news, gospel; the true message the exclusion was designed to sever the Galatians from.
usage: “they would exclude you, that ye might affect them” — Paul's exposure of the false teachers' true purpose.
“Am I therefore become your enemy, because I tell you the truth?” — the exclusion working exactly as intended.
“it is good to be zealously affected always in a good thing” — Paul's own standard for testing any such zeal.

pos: n. (the utmost point, degree, or state; a condition of great distress or peril)
etymology: Latin extremitas, from extremus, outermost, the superlative of exter, outward. An extremity is, at root, the outermost point a thing can reach — the edge beyond which there is nothing further of the same kind.
biblical_def:
Elihu's speech to Job, in the long dialogue that occupies most of the book, uses the word at a moment of careful theological correction. Job has complained that crying out to God brings no answer; Elihu's response names the actual state of Job's suffering with unusual precision: because it is not so, he hath visited in his anger; yet he knoweth it not in great extremity. The claim is subtle — Elihu does not deny that Job is suffering greatly, but he denies that Job's suffering has actually reached the extremity Job himself imagines it has, and suggests that God's silence is not indifference but a form of restraint even in the midst of real affliction.

Whatever the merits of Elihu's specific diagnosis of Job's case, the passage names something true about how suffering is experienced from the inside: extremity is not merely a matter of the pain actually endured but of how total and inescapable that pain feels to the sufferer in the moment, which is not always the same measurement. Elihu goes on to charge Job with multiplying words without knowledge, precisely because Job's own sense of extremity had begun to outrun the actual facts of his case. Scripture elsewhere is entirely willing to let a sufferer's cry from genuine extremity stand unquestioned, as in many of the Psalms; Elihu's speech is one of the rare places where an extremity claimed is itself weighed and found, in this particular instance, to have been overstated.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the utmost point or degree; the highest degree of distress, danger, or necessity; also, the outermost part.
webster_full: EXTREMITY, n. The utmost point, degree, or state; the highest degree of distress or need; the outermost part.
VISIT, v.t. To come upon, especially with judgment, affliction, or punishment; also, to go to see.
KNOW, v.t. To perceive with certainty; to have clear and certain understanding of a fact or truth.
MULTIPLY, v.t. To increase in number; to make many; here, of words spoken without corresponding substance.
AFFLICTION, n. A state of pain, distress, or misery; a trial permitted or sent by divine providence.
scriptures: Although thou sayest thou shalt not see him, yet judgment is before him; therefore trust thou in him.
But now, because it is not so, he hath visited in his anger; yet he knoweth it not in great extremity:
Therefore doth Job open his mouth in vain; he multiplieth words without knowledge.
Then they cried unto the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them out of their distresses.
corruption_summary: A sufferer's own sense of reaching an absolute extremity is treated as automatically authoritative and beyond question, when Elihu's speech to Job shows Scripture willing, in at least this one case, to weigh a claimed extremity against the actual facts and find it overstated.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; extremity still names the utmost point of distress. The principle worth recovering is the careful, unusual work Elihu's speech is doing. Most of Scripture's treatment of suffering, especially in the Psalms, takes the sufferer's own cry of extremity at face value and answers it with comfort rather than correction.

Elihu's speech to Job is one of the rare exceptions, and it is worth noting precisely because it is rare: he does not deny Job's real affliction, but he questions whether Job's sense of total abandonment matches what has actually happened, and charges him with multiplying words without knowledge as a result. Psalm 107's own testimony, that those who cried unto the LORD in their trouble were delivered out of their distresses, shows the ordinary pattern extremity is met with in Scripture; Elihu's speech is the harder, more exceptional case of a suffering man's own diagnosis of his extremity being gently, respectfully, but genuinely disputed.
roots_summary: The Hebrew behind Job 35:15's “great extremity” is an intensified idiom rather than a single fixed noun, built on words for visiting in anger and abounding trouble.
roots_lines: Hebrew idiom (Job 35:15) — the verse's “great extremity” renders a Hebrew phrase built on intensity rather than a single fixed noun, underlining how much of the verse's force is Elihu's own interpretive framing.
Hebrew paqad (H6485) — to visit, to attend to, often with judgment; the verb behind “he hath visited in his anger.”
Hebrew rabah (H7235) — to multiply, to increase; the verb behind “he multiplieth words without knowledge.”
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, justice, a legal cause; the standing matter Elihu insists is before God even in silence.
Hebrew tsarah (H6869) — distress, trouble, adversity; the standard word for the affliction Psalm 107:6 describes as met with deliverance.
usage: “yet he knoweth it not in great extremity” — Elihu's careful, disputed diagnosis of Job's own claim.
“he multiplieth words without knowledge” — Elihu's charge against an overstated extremity.
“they cried unto the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them” — the ordinary pattern extremity is met with elsewhere.

pos: v.t. (to finish or perform quickly; to put to death; to send off with speed)
etymology: Old French despeechier, from des-, undoing, and a root related to pied, foot, or to being caught — to free something from delay, sending it off quickly. In its harsher sense, the word narrowed to the quick ending of a life.
biblical_def:
Ezekiel's allegory of the two adulterous sisters, Aholah and Aholibah, standing for Samaria and Jerusalem, reaches its judgment with a phrase whose violence is deliberate rather than incidental: the company shall stone them with stones, and dispatch them with their swords; they shall slay their sons and their daughters, and burn up their houses with fire. The dispatch named here is not a euphemism softening the judgment but its stated method, a quick, decisive killing that ends the allegory's long, patiently detailed description of covenant unfaithfulness in a single, unadorned act.

The chapter's closing purpose, stated immediately after, is not merely retributive: Thus will I cause lewdness to cease out of the land, that all women may be taught not to do after your lewdness. A dispatch this severe is presented as instructive as much as punitive, a public and final judgment meant to teach a wider audience the actual cost of the covenant-breaking the allegory has spent an entire chapter describing in uncomfortable detail. Scripture's willingness to record such a judgment without softening its language is itself part of the text's argument: a covenant taken as seriously as marriage, when broken as seriously as adultery, is not treated by the prophets as a matter to be described gently.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to send off or execute with haste; also, to put to death, especially with quickness or without delay.
webster_full: DISPATCH, v.t. To perform or send off quickly; also, to kill or put to death speedily.
COVENANT, n. A solemn agreement, especially between God and his people, often figured as a marriage.
LEWDNESS, n. Lustful, unchaste conduct; gross sexual immorality; in Scripture, often a figure for covenant unfaithfulness.
ALLEGORY, n. A figurative narrative in which characters and events represent abstract or spiritual truths.
JUDGMENT, n. The act of judging; a sentence pronounced, especially the divine sentence upon sin.
scriptures: For thus saith the Lord GOD; I will bring up a company upon them, and will give them to be removed and spoiled.
And the company shall stone them with stones, and dispatch them with their swords; they shall slay their sons and their daughters, and burn up their houses with fire.
Thus will I cause lewdness to cease out of the land, that all women may be taught not to do after your lewdness.
And I will judge thee, as women that break wedlock and shed blood are judged; and I will give thee blood in fury and jealousy.
corruption_summary: Covenant unfaithfulness is treated as a private failing with limited consequence, when Ezekiel's allegory pictures its judgment in the same severe terms Scripture reserves for capital crimes, a dispatch meant to be publicly instructive, not merely privately regretted.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; to dispatch still means to finish, often violently, with speed. The principle worth recovering is why the prophets are willing to describe covenant-breaking in language this severe rather than softer, more clinical terms. Ezekiel judges the sisters as women that break wedlock and shed blood are judged, treating spiritual unfaithfulness with the same gravity Israel's law gave to adultery and bloodshed.

The stated purpose of the judgment, that all women may be taught not to do after your lewdness, refuses to let the dispatch be read as mere vengeance disconnected from any larger lesson. Scripture's severity here is not gratuitous; it is calibrated to match the seriousness of the covenant actually broken, and the text's own discomfort in the reader's ear is part of how seriously it wants covenant faithfulness to be taken in the first place.
roots_summary: Hebrew karath (H3772), to cut off, to dispatch by the sword; the verb behind “dispatch” in Ezekiel 23:47, the same root used of cutting a covenant.
roots_lines: Hebrew bathar or karath (H3772) — to cut off, to cut down; the verb underlying “dispatch,” the same root elsewhere used of cutting (making) a covenant.
Hebrew ragam (H7275) — to stone, to cast stones; the specific method of execution named alongside dispatch by the sword.
Hebrew zanah (H2181) — to commit fornication, to be a harlot; the standing verb for the covenant-breaking allegorized throughout Ezekiel 23.
Hebrew zimmah (H2154) — lewdness, wickedness, especially of a sexual nature; the word behind “lewdness” in Ezekiel 23:48.
Hebrew qana (H7065) — to be jealous, zealous; the covenant jealousy behind the judgment of Ezekiel 16:38.
usage: “the company shall stone them with stones, and dispatch them with their swords” — the judgment on covenant unfaithfulness.
“that all women may be taught not to do after your lewdness” — the instructive purpose behind the severity.
“I will judge thee, as women that break wedlock and shed blood are judged” — the same severity from Ezekiel sixteen.

pos: v.t. (to set on fire; to excite or heighten a passion or appetite beyond its proper bound)
etymology: Latin inflammare, from in-, into, and flamma, a flame. To inflame is, at root, to set something alight from within, an image English kept for both literal fire and the heated, self-feeding intensity of an unchecked appetite.
biblical_def:
Isaiah's series of prophetic woes against Judah's ruling class opens with a picture of appetite pursued past every natural stopping point: Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them! The picture is not of an occasional excess but of a whole day's structure reorganized around drink, morning to night, until the wine has done its full, self-escalating work. The word does real diagnostic work here — wine does not merely intoxicate these men, it inflames them, kindling an appetite that grows rather than being satisfied by what feeds it.

Isaiah's larger indictment, two verses later, sharpens the target further: woe unto them that are mighty to drink wine, and men of strength to mingle strong drink, a warped inversion of genuine strength spent entirely on capacity for self-indulgence. The chapter's closing observation supplies the real diagnosis behind the inflamed appetite — they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands. An inflamed appetite, in Isaiah's usage, is not merely a matter of excess; it is what fills the space in a man's attention that ought to be occupied by the work and hand of the God he has stopped considering, the fire of appetite rushing in exactly where the fire of true worship has gone out.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to set on fire; to kindle; figuratively, to excite or increase in intensity, as a passion or appetite.
webster_full: INFLAME, v.t. To set on fire; to kindle into a flame; figuratively, to rouse or excite to excessive heat or passion.
STRONG DRINK, n. Intoxicating liquor, especially as distinguished from wine in some biblical contexts; any potent alcoholic drink.
WOE, n. Grievous distress or calamity; a word of prophetic denunciation or warning.
MIGHTY, a. Possessing great power or strength, whether physical, moral, or figurative.
OPERATION, n. The act or process of operating; the exertion of power or influence producing an effect.
scriptures: Isa 5:11
Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!
Isa 5:12
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.
Isa 5:22
Woe unto them that are mighty to drink wine, and men of strength to mingle strong drink:
Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth itself aright.
corruption_summary: An inflamed appetite is treated as a private matter of personal moderation, unrelated to worship, when Isaiah ties the whole condition directly to men who no longer regard the work of the LORD or consider the operation of his hands.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; to inflame still means to kindle beyond a proper measure. The principle worth recovering is Isaiah's own diagnosis of the cause, not merely the symptom. The men in this woe are not condemned simply for drinking, but for reorganizing an entire day, morning to night, around an appetite that grows the more it is fed.

The chapter's own explanation for how such a condition arises is not primarily physiological but spiritual: they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands. An inflamed appetite fills exactly the space that attention to God's own work was meant to occupy, and Isaiah's woe is aimed less at the wine itself than at the emptied, unconsidering heart the wine has been allowed to rush into and inflame without any competing claim on the man's attention.
roots_summary: Hebrew dalaq (H1814), to burn, to kindle, to pursue hotly; the verb behind “inflame” in Isaiah 5:11, carrying a sense of hot, relentless pursuit.
roots_lines: Hebrew dalaq (H1814) — to burn, to be kindled, to pursue hotly; the verb rendered “inflame” in Isaiah 5:11, elsewhere used of a hot, relentless chase.
Hebrew shekar (H7941) — strong drink, an intoxicating beverage distinct from wine; the object of the early pursuit in this woe.
Hebrew yayin (H3196) — wine; the standard word paired with strong drink throughout this chapter's indictment.
Hebrew naba't (H5027, negated) — to regard, to look at attentively; explicitly denied of these men toward the work of the LORD.
Hebrew ma'aseh (H4639) — a work, a deed, an action; the standing word for the LORD's own doings these men fail to consider.
usage: “that continue until night, till wine inflame them” — Isaiah's picture of an appetite pursued past every stopping point.
“they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands” — the diagnosis behind the inflamed appetite.
“Look not thou upon the wine when it is red” — the standing wisdom warning against the same appetite.

pos: a. (capable of being inhabited; fit for habitation or dwelling)
etymology: Latin habitabilis, from habitare, to dwell, itself from habere, to have or hold. The habitable part of a place is, at root, the part able to be held and dwelt in by living inhabitants.
biblical_def:
Wisdom's own speech in Proverbs eight, describing her presence at the creation of the world before the mountains were settled or the fountains established, arrives at a striking claim about where her deepest delight was actually found: Rejoicing in the habitable part of his earth; and my delights were with the sons of men. Wisdom does not describe her joy as centered on the vast, uninhabited cosmos alone, the depths or the heavens or the foundations of the earth mentioned earlier in the same speech; her rejoicing narrows and focuses specifically on the habitable part, the portion of creation actually made for men to dwell in.

The parallel half of the verse makes the focus explicit: my delights were with the sons of men. Wisdom, present with God before any of the world's works of old, as one brought up with him, daily his delight, chooses in the very same breath to locate her own delight not merely in the grandeur of the whole created order but specifically in the habitable earth made for human dwelling and in mankind itself. It is a striking claim for a book devoted mostly to practical instruction: the divine Wisdom that helped establish the entire cosmos found her particular joy exactly where ordinary people actually live, work, and dwell, rather than in some more rarefied or inaccessible corner of creation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): capable of being inhabited; suitable for the residence of human beings.
webster_full: HABITABLE, a. Capable of being inhabited; fit to be dwelt in; suitable for residence.
REJOICE, v.i. To feel joy or gladness in a high degree; to exult; to be delighted.
WISDOM, n. The right use of knowledge; the faculty of discerning and pursuing the best ends by the best means, personified in Proverbs as present at creation.
FOUNDATION, n. The base or lower part of a structure; figuratively, the fixed and original establishment of the earth.
DELIGHT, n. A high degree of pleasure or satisfaction of mind; joy taken in a person or thing.
scriptures: Pro 8:22
The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old.
Pro 8:30
Then I was by him, as one brought up with him: and I was daily his delight, rejoicing always before him;
Pro 8:31
Rejoicing in the habitable part of his earth; and my delights were with the sons of men.

For thus saith the LORD that created the heavens; God himself that formed the earth and made it; he hath established it, he created it not in vain, he formed it to be inhabited: I am the LORD; and there is none else.
corruption_summary: Wisdom is imagined as an abstract, detached faculty removed from ordinary human life, when Proverbs eight has Wisdom herself declare her deepest delight to be located precisely in the habitable earth and among the sons of men.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; habitable still names what is fit for dwelling. The principle worth recovering is the deliberate focus of Wisdom's own testimony in this passage. Having just described her presence before the mountains, the fountains, and the foundations of the earth, she narrows her rejoicing specifically to the habitable part, the portion actually made for human dwelling, rather than resting her delight in creation's grandest or least accessible reaches.

Isaiah's later statement supplies the theology behind Wisdom's own preference: God formed the earth not in vain, he formed it to be inhabited. A habitable world is not a lesser or incidental byproduct of creation but part of its original purpose, and Wisdom's delight in that habitable earth and in the sons of men who dwell there models the same priority the LORD Himself is said to have built into creation from the start.
roots_summary: Hebrew tebel (H8398), the habitable world, the earth as a dwelling place; the noun behind “the habitable part” in Proverbs 8:31.
roots_lines: Hebrew tebel (H8398) — the habitable world, the earth considered as a dwelling place; the noun rendered “the habitable part” in Proverbs 8:31.
Hebrew sha'shua (H8191) — delight, pleasure; the noun behind “delights” in the same verse, Wisdom's own joy.
Hebrew qanah (H7069) — to possess, acquire, or bring forth; the verb behind “possessed me” in Proverbs 8:22.
Hebrew amon (H542, disputed) — a master workman, or one brought up; the term describing Wisdom's own relationship to the LORD in verse 30.
Hebrew yatsar (H3335) — to form, to fashion; the verb behind Isaiah 45:18's declaration that the earth was formed to be inhabited.
usage: “Rejoicing in the habitable part of his earth; and my delights were with the sons of men” — Wisdom's own declared joy.
“I was daily his delight, rejoicing always before him” — Wisdom's standing before the LORD at creation.
“he formed it to be inhabited” — the theology behind a habitable earth as God's own original intent.

pos: a. (foreign in speech or manner; uncivilized; in the Authorized Version, simply non-Greek-speaking)
etymology: Greek barbaros, originally an imitative word for the unintelligible babble of a foreign tongue — ba-ba-ba — used by Greek speakers of anyone who did not speak Greek, without necessarily implying cruelty or savagery.
biblical_def:
Luke's account of Paul's shipwreck on the island of Melita records the reception the survivors actually received from the local inhabitants, using this word in a way that upends the assumption its later English sense might invite: the barbarous people shewed us no little kindness: for they kindled a fire, and received us every one, because of the present rain, and because of the cold. The word names only what it named in Luke's own Greek — non-Greek-speaking islanders, foreign in tongue and custom to Paul's traveling companions — and immediately, in the very same sentence, credits them with kindness that a shipwrecked company of Roman prisoners and soldiers had no particular claim upon.

The scene that follows sharpens the reversal further. When a viper fastens on Paul's hand, these same barbarians conclude he must be a murderer whom vengeance would not suffer to live, a judgment that turns out to be entirely wrong; and when Paul suffers no harm, they swing to the opposite extreme and call him a god. Luke records both misjudgments without mockery, letting the islanders' theological confusion sit alongside their genuine, costly hospitality. A people barbarous only in the sense of speaking a different tongue are shown capable of real kindness and real, if mistaken, religious reasoning — Scripture using the word purely as Luke's own culture used it, without smuggling in the harsher sense English later gave the same term.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): uncivilized; foreign in speech; used originally of any people whose language was unintelligible to the Greeks or Romans.
webster_full: BARBAROUS, a. Uncivilized; foreign or strange in speech; in ancient usage, simply not Greek-speaking, without necessarily implying cruelty.
KINDNESS, n. Good will; benevolence; a disposition to do good and to please others.
SHIPWRECK, n. The destruction of a ship by storm, rocks, or other disaster at sea.
VIPER, n. A poisonous serpent; used figuratively in Scripture of malice or deadly danger.
VENGEANCE, n. Punishment inflicted in retribution for an injury or offense; retributive justice.
scriptures: Act 28:1
And when they were escaped, then they knew that the island was called Melita.
Act 28:2
And the barbarous people shewed us no little kindness: for they kindled a fire, and received us every one, because of the present rain, and because of the cold.
Act 28:4

And when the barbarians saw the venomous beast hang on his hand, they said among themselves, No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he hath escaped the sea, yet vengeance suffereth not to live.
Act 28:6

Howbeit they looked when he should have swollen, or fallen down dead suddenly: but after they had looked a great while, and saw no harm come to him, they changed their minds, and said that he was a god.
corruption_summary: Barbarous is read back into Scripture with its modern sense of savage or cruel, when Luke's own Greek uses the word purely to mean non-Greek-speaking, immediately crediting these very islanders with real, costly kindness.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition so much as an anachronistic misreading, importing English's later, harsher sense of the word back into a Greek term that originally meant nothing more than foreign in speech. The principle worth recovering is how carefully Luke's own account undercuts any assumption that barbarous meant uncivilized in the pejorative sense: these barbarians shewed no little kindness, kindled a fire, and received a boatload of storm-battered strangers with no obligation to do so.

Their subsequent misjudgments about Paul, first as a murderer marked by vengeance, then, on the opposite extreme, as a god, are recorded not as evidence of savagery but of ordinary religious reasoning working with incomplete information, exactly the kind of theological confusion any culture unfamiliar with the true God might reach for. Scripture's own use of the word offers no license for treating a foreign tongue as evidence of a lesser capacity for genuine kindness or careful, if mistaken, thought.
roots_summary: Greek barbaros (G915), a foreigner, one speaking an unintelligible tongue; the adjective behind “barbarous” and “barbarians” in Acts 28, imitative in origin of unintelligible foreign speech.
roots_lines: Greek barbaros (G915) — a foreigner, a non-Greek-speaker; an imitative word for the sound of unintelligible speech, without inherent moral judgment.
Greek philanthropia (G5363) — love of mankind, kindness, humanity; the quality Luke elsewhere uses of similar hospitality (Acts 28:2 uses a related idea, kindness).
Greek echidna (G2191) — a viper, a venomous serpent; the creature that fastened on Paul's hand.
Greek dike (G1349) — justice, vengeance, retribution personified; the power the islanders believed was pursuing Paul.
Greek theos (G2316) — God, a god; the opposite conclusion the same islanders reached once Paul suffered no harm.
usage: “the barbarous people shewed us no little kindness” — Luke's own correction of any assumption about the word's meaning.
“No doubt this man is a murderer, whom... vengeance suffereth not to live” — their first, mistaken theological judgment.
“they changed their minds, and said that he was a god” — their second, equally mistaken conclusion.

pos: a. (marked by politeness and gracious respect toward others; well-mannered)
etymology: Old French corteis, from cort, a royal court — behavior fit for the presence of a king, the polished manner a courtier was expected to show. To be courteous is, at root, to carry oneself as one accustomed to a royal court's own standard of respect.
biblical_def:
Peter's instruction to a persecuted church, gathering several virtues into a single compact list, closes with this word placed deliberately alongside others that might seem, on the surface, more obviously weighty: Finally, be ye all of one mind, having compassion one of another, love as brethren, be pitiful, be courteous. Courtesy sits here not as a minor social nicety appended to greater virtues but as their natural completion — compassion, brotherly love, and pity that fail to express themselves in ordinary courteous manner have not yet finished becoming what Peter is actually describing.

The verse immediately following makes plain that this courtesy is not merely a matter of good manners toward the agreeable; it is meant to survive contact with real provocation: Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing. A courtesy that only holds when courtesy is easily returned is not the virtue Peter has in mind; the whole passage is addressed to believers under real pressure, and courteous conduct, held even under railing, is Peter's chosen name for compassion that has learned to keep its ordinary, gracious shape precisely when provocation would make rudeness feel justified.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): of polite and gracious manners; civil; well-bred; respectful and considerate in behavior toward others.
webster_full: COURTEOUS, a. Of polished manners; civil; complaisant; respectful and considerate in one's bearing toward others.
PITIFUL, a. Full of pity; compassionate; tender toward the suffering or distressed.
COMPASSION, n. A feeling of sorrow for the distress of another, joined with a desire to help.
RAIL, v.i. To use reproachful or scornful language; to speak abusively.
BLESSING, n. An invocation of divine favor upon another; also, a gift or benefit bestowed.
scriptures: Finally, be ye all of one mind, having compassion one of another, love as brethren, be pitiful, be courteous:
Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing.
Tit 3:2
To speak evil of no man, to be no brawlers, but gentle, shewing all meekness unto all men.
Col 4:6
Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.
corruption_summary: Courtesy is dismissed as a superficial social nicety beneath the weight of real virtue, when Peter places it as the natural, practical completion of compassion and brotherly love, specifically tested by whether it survives railing and provocation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; courteous still names gracious, well-mannered conduct toward others. The principle worth recovering is Peter's own placement of the word, at the end of a list of substantial internal virtues, as though courtesy were simply what compassion, brotherly love, and pity look like once they have found their outward, everyday expression.

The immediately following instruction, not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing, shows that Peter's courtesy is not the easy, low-cost politeness offered only when nothing threatens it. Titus's parallel instruction, to speak evil of no man, to be no brawlers, but gentle, and Colossians' command that speech always be seasoned with grace, confirm the same New Testament pattern: courteous conduct is measured precisely by whether it holds under provocation, which is exactly the condition Peter's persecuted readers were actually facing.
roots_summary: Greek philophron (G5391), friendly-minded, courteous; the rare compound adjective behind “courteous” in 1 Peter 3:8, from philos, friend, and phren, mind.
roots_lines: Greek philophron (G5391) — friendly-minded, courteous, kindly disposed; a rare compound, used only at 1 Peter 3:8 in the New Testament.
Greek eusplagchnos (G2155) — tenderhearted, compassionate, literally of good bowels; the word behind “pitiful” in the same verse.
Greek homophron (G3675) — of one mind, likeminded; the first virtue in Peter's list, the shared disposition courtesy expresses outwardly.
Greek loidoria (G3059) — railing, reviling, abusive speech; the provocation courteous conduct is specifically tested against.
Greek eulogia (G2129) — a blessing, good speech; the opposite response Peter commands in place of returned railing.
usage: “be pitiful, be courteous” — the outward completion of Peter's list of inward virtues.
“Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing” — the real test of that courtesy.
“Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt” — the same standard from Colossians.
